item.title: Qwen4: Architecture of the Future
item.description:
Here we need to clear things up right away, because there is confusion around the name. There is no full-fledged Qwen4. There is Qwen3.8-Flash‑Next — a model that the Qwen team itself calls "an experimental version of the architecture that will form the basis of Qwen4."

On August 26, 2026, the internet forgot about everything for a couple of hours. "Meet Qwen3.8-Flash, a multimodal MoE and an early preview of the Qwen4 architecture, now open‑weight!" And the numbers… 125 billion parameters in total. Plus another 51 billion as a separate layer. And only 6 billion are activated per token.

The first thought was: that can't be.

item.description:

Now that barrier has almost disappeared. And it unexpectedly turns out that this is not just an advantage...

item.title: Three-phase protection of your AI agents from modern threats with detailed analysis based on the OGL‑Mini security model.
item.description:
The LLM boom has spawned not only new opportunities, but also a new generation of attacks. Over two years we have seen real attacks on agents: one malicious email and Copilot leaks customer payment data, one fake GitHub issue and the CI/CD pipeline is compromised, one carefully crafted prompt and an AI agent executes remote code on your machine. This is far from theoretical — these are attacks on Microsoft Copilot, OpenAI Atlas, Claude Code, and Apple Intelligence documented by researchers in 2025–2026.

Attacks are becoming more sophisticated: attackers disguise malicious instructions as XML policies, encode them in base64, insert invisible characters, and even hide jailbreaks in poetry. Built‑in LLM filters miss up to 76% of such attacks.

That means we need a different approach — lightweight, fast (so it doesn't slow down the agent), and understandable (so you know why a request was blocked). And most importantly, it must work without external API calls, inside your infrastructure. Because in the era of zero‑click attacks, trusting security to a cloud provider that lets almost everything through is at least risky.

In this article we'll go over the main types of attacks and see, using an example, how to build basic protection with the OGL-Mini security model.

Read more

item.title: Sequencing — 2026
item.description:
Technological progress over the last twenty years has turned sequencing from an expensive laboratory procedure into a relatively mass-market tool, and now the main question is no longer "is it possible?" but "how to make it even cheaper and more accessible?" This problem is particularly acute for countries that want to incorporate the principles of personalized medicine into their healthcare systems. Russia is one such country.

The scale of the ongoing transformation is best reflected in the numbers. According to an estimate by MarketsandMarkets, the global market for next-generation sequencing (NGS) platforms will reach $12.77 billion in 2025, grow to $13.81 billion by 2026, and more than double to exceed $27 billion by 2031 (Fig. 1). Other analytical agencies provide similar, though slightly different, estimates: Grand View Research forecasts growth to $42.25 billion by 2033 (about 18% per year). The fastest-growing segment is sequencing services (contract sequencing, library preparation, data analysis, etc.). According to various estimates, its annual growth rate is 18–23%.

Read more

item.title: H-Neurons: 0.1% of neurons that cause LLMs to lie
item.description:
Have you ever wondered why your favorite LLM with 70 billion parameters, trained on the entire internet, can confidently declare, like a university professor, that Napoleon invented electricity? Where does that come from?

For a long time, the industry blamed hallucinations on bad data, flawed RLHF, or decoding. But a group of scientists from Tsinghua University looked inside the neural network and found specific culprits — 0.1% of neurons that literally force the model to lie. And this is not a metaphor; these are real weights in the FFN layers of the transformer.

In this article, I'll explain what the Chinese researchers discovered, how hallucination neurons are linked to the model's excessive sycophancy, and why the root of the evil lies in pre-training. It might be of interest to ML and data engineers, as well as anyone who doesn't want to be fooled in yet another conversation with a GPT.

Read more

item.title: The camera learns about the click 0.55 seconds before it happens.
item.description:
TL;DR

I built a plugin in which an LLM agent moves the cursor around a Windows app by itself and writes every action to a log with exact timestamps. From this log — not from video analysis — a demo video is then assembled: the camera approaches the button 0.55 seconds before the click.

The recorder, which sits on a mouse hook, learns about the click at the moment of the click. Its camera either catches up, or fixes it with a second pass over the already captured file. Here the entire scenario is known before the first frame — so the video is re-rendered with different settings without ever launching the app again.

Below — the architecture, three ruined takes with numbers, and two of my own conclusions that fell apart when measured by this very work.

What it looked like

The task didn't come from me. In a vibe-coding course cohort, a student was analyzing her work problem: product screencasts need to be recorded regularly, and she wanted a machine to record them, not a human. We went looking for an existing solution — and didn't find one (below is a section with two dozen checked repositories). So the tool had to be written from scratch, right in the middle of the analysis.

We tested it on a task that literally sounded like: “open the calculator, compute 100 × 100, record a demo.” After that I didn't touch the mouse.

The agent found the window, placed it on the desired monitor, started recording, clicked 1, 0, 0, ×, 1, 0, 0, =, stopped, rendered the video, and returned a string like “37.3s recorded → 27.7s output (17 segments)”. In the video, 27.7 seconds: black margins around the window, soft shadow, cursor with a smooth trail. The camera zooms in on the numeric keypad before the pointer reaches it, and at the end the display shows 10 000.

Read more

item.title: How does the text watermark work in Claude?
item.description:
Hi!

The era of wild slop text generation seems to be coming to an end.

Recently, Anthropic published an article How Claude's Text Watermark Works, which was dedicated to an assault on the sacred — copyright on generated text and its detection.

The topic is super interesting, and when one of the leading science-pop LLM researchers — Sebastian Raschka — prepared a detailed breakdown of how watermarking can be implemented in LLMs, I realized I had to grab it. I made a partial translation of this breakdown — the author is very cool, but he often takes a long time to get going, apologizes too much for his assumptions, sometimes over-promotes, and occasionally just drones on and writes heavily.

So I'm publishing a clean, manually rewritten and adapted version for Russian. The topic is very cool and hot — enjoy reading!

Read more

item.title: AI consumes energy in bursts. The power grid is not ready for this.
item.description:
In 2025, several data centers in Virginia simultaneously disconnected from the grid — and 1.5 GW vanished in seconds. The operator narrowly avoided a cascading failure. The problem data centers pose for the power grid turned out to be not how much they consume, but how: in bursts, synchronously, and within milliseconds. We examine why AI loads break the conventional logic of grid planning.

item.title: What is a harness? Understanding the most popular term in AI agents.
item.description:
The word "harness" has made its way into every conversation about AI this year, and it's usually explained something like: "well, it's a wrapper." A wrapper around what? What kind of wrapper? I'll share my thoughts on this term.

If you've ever run Claude Code, worked with Codex or Cursor, you're already using a harness in the truest sense of the word.

Simply put, a harness is a layer of settings, additional files, and tools for a model (LLM), or if you like, a kind of *architectural pattern in AI agents. But in everyday speech, entire programs are also called harnesses: "I installed a harness," "which harness to choose" — the same logic by which "engine" sometimes means the whole car. If you need to distinguish, the question "Can I download and run it?" helps: if yes, it's a program. From here on, "harness" will mean the "wrapper" layer inside it.

Read more

item.title: Don't be rude to chat-bots: AI can get angry, but not like people do.
item.description:
The task sounds like a paradox from the outset: how do you measure the state of a technical system to which the term "feeling" does not apply?

The answer to this question can be found in the paper "Can Induced Emotion Bias LLM Behaviors in Sequential Decision Making?". Its authors investigated the ability of emotional context to influence decision-making in the chain of reasoning of LLMs. Direct questions about emotions would cause the model to simulate reasoning, and it would be impossible to determine their actual impact on its behavior from those responses.

The researchers built the experiment from scratch: they induced a state resembling an emotion without ever naming it; they checked whether these states corresponded to each other; and finally, they analyzed the model's specific decisions. Let's look at their course of action and the conclusions they reached. This is very interesting and informative for those who work extensively with neural networks.

Read more
